title: When Are the lac Genes High?

scenes.tts: Why does a bacterium offered glucose and lactose postpone the lactose genes? Follow one promoter inside a single cell. Two signals must line up before its output becomes high.
scenes.caption: Why does a bacterium offered glucose and lactose postpone the lactose genes? Follow one promoter inside a single cell. Two signals must line up before its output becomes high.
scenes.visual: Hook picture. A large schematic E. coli cell fills the frame. Blue glucose and yellow lactose blocks enter together. Inside, one DNA rail carries a large expression meter. Glucose is used while the meter stays low; lactose waits beside a question mark. Label the whole diagram ‘schematic’.
scenes.narration: Why does a bacterium offered glucose and lactose postpone the lactose genes? Follow one promoter inside a single cell. Two signals must line up before its output becomes high.

scenes.visual: Keep the same cell and DNA rail moving with gentle membrane drift. Add the title ‘When Are the lac Genes High?’ for two seconds, then dissolve it without clearing the cell.

scenes.tts: The rail carries the lac Z, lac Y, and lac A genes after one promoter. Polymerase can copy them into one messenger RNA. Together, these genes form one operon and produce one messenger with three coding regions. But a red repressor clamp grips the operator beside that promoter. The clamp blocks transcription.
scenes.caption: The rail carries the lacZ, lacY, and lacA genes after one promoter. Polymerase can copy them into one messenger RNA. Together, these genes form one operon and produce one messenger with three coding regions. But a red repressor clamp grips the operator beside that promoter. The clamp blocks transcription.
scenes.visual: Zoom the carried DNA rail to fill most of the frame. Green lacZ, lacY, and lacA blocks unfold from one promoter. A white polymerase cartoon approaches. A red clamp labelled ‘repressor’ closes around an orange operator block and stops the polymerase. Keep all geometry schematic.
scenes.narration: The rail carries the lacZ, lacY, and lacA genes after one promoter. Polymerase can copy them into one messenger RNA. Together, these genes form one operon and produce one messenger with three coding regions. But a red repressor clamp grips the operator beside that promoter. The clamp blocks transcription.

scenes.tts: Yellow lactose crosses the membrane through permease. Beta-galactosidase turns a little lactose into allolactose, the natural inducer. Lactose itself is not the inducer; conversion matters. Allolactose reshapes the clamp and lowers its affinity for the operator. The clamp loosens, so polymerase can move.
scenes.caption: Yellow lactose crosses the membrane through permease. β-Galactosidase turns a little lactose into allolactose, the natural inducer. Lactose itself is not the inducer; conversion matters. Allolactose reshapes the clamp and lowers its affinity for the operator. The clamp loosens, so polymerase can move.
scenes.visual: Pull back to include the membrane. Yellow lactose blocks pass a yellow permease gate. A green β-galactosidase tool transforms one lactose block into a labelled yellow allolactose badge, without molecular structure. The badge docks on the red clamp; its jaws open and drift from the orange operator. Polymerase advances and RNA grows.
scenes.narration: Yellow lactose crosses the membrane through permease. β-Galactosidase turns a little lactose into allolactose, the natural inducer. Lactose itself is not the inducer; conversion matters. Allolactose reshapes the clamp and lowers its affinity for the operator. The clamp loosens, so polymerase can move.

scenes.tts: This creates a loop. Permease and beta-galactosidase help produce the signal that increases their own production. The loop can amplify a small beginning into stronger production when conditions allow. Basal leak supplies a few starting proteins. So the switch is not perfectly binary.
scenes.caption: This creates a loop. Permease and β-galactosidase help produce the signal that increases their own production. The loop can amplify a small beginning into stronger production when conditions allow. Basal leak supplies a few starting proteins. So the switch is not perfectly binary.
scenes.visual: Carry the membrane gate, enzyme tool, and DNA rail into a circular arrow. A few small permease gates and enzyme tools appear before induction, labelled ‘basal leak’. The expression meter rises from a faint baseline rather than from zero. Slow particles continue moving inside the cell.

scenes.tts: Removing the brake is only one input. The promoter is weak by itself. Teal C A P, carrying cyclic A M P, docks upstream. It contacts polymerase and helps transcription start. The activator does not remove repressor. Each regulator has a different job. This is positive control.
scenes.caption: Removing the brake is only one input. The promoter is weak by itself. Teal CAP, carrying cyclic AMP, docks upstream. It contacts polymerase and helps transcription start. The activator does not remove repressor. Each regulator has a different job. This is positive control.
scenes.visual: Return to the DNA rail with the red clamp open. Polymerase tries to dock and slips back while the meter stays modest. A teal CAP shape carrying a small teal cyclic AMP badge docks upstream and extends an arm to polymerase. Polymerase locks in place and advances; the meter rises.
scenes.narration: Removing the brake is only one input. The promoter is weak by itself. Teal CAP, carrying cyclic AMP, docks upstream. It contacts polymerase and helps transcription start. The activator does not remove repressor. Each regulator has a different job. This is positive control.

scenes.tts: Glucose changes both inputs. In the classic account, cyclic A M P is lower when glucose is plentiful. How much this matters in living cells is debated. Glucose uptake also makes a transport protein block permease. Less lactose enters, so less allolactose releases the repressor.
scenes.caption: Glucose changes both inputs. In the classic account, cyclic AMP is lower when glucose is plentiful. How much this matters in living cells is debated. Glucose uptake also makes a transport protein block permease. Less lactose enters, so less allolactose releases the repressor.
scenes.visual: Blue glucose blocks flow through a separate gate. The teal cyclic AMP badge becomes sparse and CAP docks less often; label this branch ‘classic account’. Simultaneously, a blue transport-system shape slides onto the yellow permease gate and narrows it. Yellow lactose flow slows, allolactose badges diminish, and the red clamp closes more often.
scenes.narration: Glucose changes both inputs. In the classic account, cyclic AMP is lower when glucose is plentiful. How much this matters in living cells is debated. Glucose uptake also makes a transport protein block permease. Less lactose enters, so less allolactose releases the repressor.

scenes.tts: Now predict one case. Lactose is present, but glucose is also plentiful. Will the expression meter reach high, or stop below it? Hold both signals in view.
scenes.caption: Now predict one case. Lactose is present, but glucose is also plentiful. Will the expression meter reach high, or stop below it? Hold both signals in view.
scenes.visual: Show yellow lactose and blue glucose together around the same cell. Keep the red clamp flickering between loose and bound, CAP docking infrequently, and the permease partly blocked. Place a large question above a neutral expression meter.
scenes.narration: Now predict one case. Lactose is present, but glucose is also plentiful. Will the expression meter reach high, or stop below it? Hold both signals in view.

scenes.visual: Keep the prediction question and neutral meter visible. The two sugar streams and membrane drift continue slowly, but do not reveal the meter level.

scenes.tts: The output is reduced, not high and not necessarily absent. Some inducer may release the brake, but activation is weaker and lactose entry is inhibited. The two controls combine without becoming a perfect switch.
scenes.caption: The output is reduced, not high and not necessarily absent. Some inducer may release the brake, but activation is weaker and lactose entry is inhibited. The two controls combine without becoming a perfect switch.
scenes.visual: Move the meter smoothly to a middle band labelled ‘reduced’. Show occasional polymerase passes, never a crossed-out gene. Keep ‘classic account’ beside the CAP branch and ‘inducer exclusion’ beside the partly blocked permease.
scenes.narration: The output is reduced, not high and not necessarily absent. Some inducer may release the brake, but activation is weaker and lactose entry is inhibited. The two controls combine without becoming a perfect switch.

scenes.tts: Without lactose, the repressor keeps expression very low, even when glucose is scarce. With both sugars, expression is reduced. Only lactose with scarce glucose releases the brake and supplies strong activation together. This table predicts expression levels, not whether every cell behaves identically.
scenes.caption: Without lactose, the repressor keeps expression very low, even when glucose is scarce. With both sugars, expression is reduced. scenes.visual: Transform the single cell into a two-by-two schematic grid. Use yellow lactose across columns and blue glucose down rows. Animate meters to ‘very low’, ‘very low’, ‘reduced’, and ‘high’. Then enlarge the high cell, carrying its open red clamp and docked teal CAP into the centre.
scenes.narration: Without lactose, the repressor keeps expression very low, even when glucose is scarce. With both sugars, expression is reduced. scenes.tts: The promoter is reading two conditions, not naming a preferred food by itself. Keep the scope clear: this rule describes high expression in wild-type E. coli under the lesson's standard model. In the lab, a synthetic inducer can stand in for lactose.
scenes.caption: The promoter is reading two conditions, not naming a preferred food by itself. Keep the scope clear: this rule describes high expression in wild-type E. coli under the lesson's standard model. In the lab, a synthetic inducer can stand in for lactose.
scenes.visual: Hold the enlarged high-expression cell. The red repressor remains off the orange operator, teal CAP remains docked, and the meter remains high. Bring the yellow lactose and ‘glucose scarce’ labels together above the promoter.
scenes.narration: The promoter is reading two conditions, not naming a preferred food by itself. Keep the scope clear: this rule describes high expression in wild-type E. coli under the lesson's standard model. In the lab, a synthetic inducer can stand in for lactose.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only, centred large on the dark background: 'In wild-type E. coli, high lac expression requires lactose and scarce glucose.'
